chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Isa, from Ibn Mahboub, from Abdullah ibn Sinan, from Abdullah ibn Suleyman, who said:

I asked Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him) about the cheese, so he said to me: 'You have asked me about a food that I love.' Then he gave the boy a dirham and said: 'O boy, buy us some cheese and call for the meal.' So we had lunch with him, and the cheese was brought. He ate and we ate with him. When we finished the meal, I said to him: 'What do you say about the cheese?' He said to me: 'Did you not see me eating it?' I said: 'Yes, but I like to hear it from you.' He said: 'I will inform you about the cheese and other things: everything that contains both permissible and prohibited elements is permissible for you until you recognize the prohibited part with your own eye, then you leave it.'
ai.seo_question: What is the Shia ruling on food items that contain both halal and haram elements?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi establishes the principle of 'al-asl al-suhha' (the default state of purity) for food, illustrating that mixed ingredients are permissible until the specific prohibited element is identified. Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) combines practical demonstration with legal reasoning, showing that the presence of a minor prohibited component (like rennet from a non-Zabiha animal) does not render the entire food haram unless its distinct nature is known. This serves as a foundational text in Shia fiqh for resolving doubts regarding food ingredients in daily life.
